title: History: Teach It and Learn from It
author: Douglas Carnine
summary: Douglas Carnine revisits a 30-year-old research program on teaching U.S. history to show that today's heated debates -- Wexler's content knowledge argument vs. Bassett/ Shiffman's critique of primary-source over-use -- were partly answered decades ago and then forgotten. Five studies using Carnine's experimental 'Understanding U.S. History' textbook found that students using it included more historical facts and concepts with fewer misconceptions in essays, scored higher on knowledge tests, learned vocabulary faster, and retained more content. The textbook was built around six design principles from Theory of Instruction: primed background knowledge, big ideas, conspicuous strategies, strategic integration, mediated scaffolding, and judicious review. The three-phase instructional sequence -- (1) Acquisition (primed background knowledge), (2) Organization (connecting facts to big ideas through strategies and scaffolding with judicious review), (3) Application (writing, problem-solving, and primary source analysis) -- shows why skipping phases predictably fails: primary sources work after preparation, not instead of it. Memorization is not the goal but is indispensable. The professional lesson: education doesn't preserve its own learning and must build cumulative knowledge bases for content areas just as it is beginning to do for literacy.
points: * Five studies found students using the knowledge-rich, sequenced experimental textbook scored higher on knowledge tests, learned vocabulary faster, wrote essays with more facts and fewer misconceptions, and retained more content over time -- including students with learning disabilities. * The six design principles from Theory of Instruction: primed background knowledge, big ideas, conspicuous strategies, strategic integration, mediated scaffolding, and judicious review -- anticipated today's knowledge-vs-skills debate by thirty years. * Three-phase instructional sequence: Acquisition (build background knowledge first), Organization (connect facts to big ideas with scaffolding and distributed review), Application (use primary sources AFTER preparation, not instead of it). * Primary sources require preparation to work: novices who encounter primary sources without prior content knowledge experience cognitive overload, shallow analysis, and misinterpretation; historians read sources effectively because they already have rich background knowledge and interpretive routines. * The professional lesson: education repeatedly forgets what it has already learned; without cumulative knowledge bases for content areas, the field will continue to rediscover old insights and reinvent the wheel.
quotes: Every time I read current arguments about history and social studies instruction, I have the same reaction: we have been here before.
The essential question was never facts or sources. The essential question is: How do we build organized knowledge that makes analysis possible?
Skipping phases leads to predictable failure. Stopping at acquisition prevents students from using what they know.
Primary sources work after preparation, not instead of it.
Memorization is not the goal -- but it is indispensable.

education does not preserve its own learning. Without a cumulative knowledge base for content areas such as history, science, and literature, the field will continue to rediscover what it already knew, repeat old debates, reinvent the wheel.
Until education learns to remember, it will remain condemned to forget.
